title: How to Tie a Tie: 4 Knots, Step by Step
hook: Interview tomorrow, a wedding on Saturday, and you still can't tie a tie? Don't worry, it is much easier than it looks. In the next few minutes, you'll learn four classic knots, from the quick four-in-hand to the full Windsor, one clear move at a time. No tie-tying experience is needed, and you can follow along with any tie you own, plus a few helpful extras.
intro: Every tie knot uses the same idea. The wide end of the tie does all the work, while the narrow end hangs still. Once you learn the setup, each knot is just a different sequence of crossing, wrapping and threading. We'll go from the simplest knot to the most formal one. Stand in front of a mirror, take your time, and remember that even people who tie a tie every day needed a few tries at the beginning. Don't worry about speed at first, because accuracy comes before speed.
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. A shirt with a collar, buttoned up. A necktie, of course. A mirror, so you can see what your hands are doing. And a few minutes of patience. If you can, practice with an old tie first, so there's no pressure on your good one. Choose a tie that isn't too thick for your first tries.
heroImagePrompt: Hands tying a navy blue necktie around the collar of a crisp white shirt, close-up in a bright bedroom, shallow depth of field, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Set up your collar and tie
steps.narration: Step one. Stand in front of a mirror with your top shirt button done up and your collar raised. Drape the tie around your neck, with the seam facing in. Place the wide end on your right and the narrow end on your left. For most men, the narrow tip should rest just above your belly button, so the wide end hangs much lower. In every knot, only the wide end moves, and the narrow end stays still. Getting this setup right is half the job, so check the lengths before you tie. If your shirt collar is stiff, loosen it slightly. Keep your shoulders relaxed and look straight into the mirror.
steps.tip: Narrow tip near your belly button
steps.mistake: Starting with both ends the same length
steps.imagePrompt: A navy necktie draped around the raised collar of a white shirt, wide end hanging lower than the narrow end, soft window light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: The four-in-hand knot
steps.narration: Step two. This is the quickest, most everyday knot. Cross the wide end over the front of the narrow end, to the left. Pass it behind the narrow end and out to the right. Carry it across the front again to the left. Now push it up through the neck loop from underneath, and down through the loop you just made in the front. Pull the wide end down gently to tighten, then slide the knot up to your collar. The result is a slim, slightly asymmetrical knot. It takes about thirty seconds once you've practiced it a few times, and it suits most shirts and most occasions.
steps.tip: Great for slim ties and narrow collars
steps.mistake: Pulling the narrow end to tighten
steps.imagePrompt: A close-up of a finished four-in-hand knot on a striped tie against a pale blue shirt, soft light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: The half Windsor knot
steps.narration: Step three. The half Windsor is neater and more balanced, so it works well for work. Cross the wide end over the front, to the left, then pass it under the narrow end and out to the right. Now bring it up through the center toward the neck loop, feed it through the loop and out to the left. Carry it across the front to the right, push it up into the neck loop from underneath, and bring it down through the loop at the front. Tighten gently. Because it uses a bit more fabric than the four-in-hand, it looks best with medium-weight ties.
steps.tip: Balanced and perfect for office wear
steps.mistake: Rushing and crossing the wrong way
steps.imagePrompt: A neat triangular half Windsor knot on a dark red tie, worn with a white shirt, close-up, soft studio light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: The full Windsor knot
steps.narration: Step four. The full Windsor is the biggest, most symmetrical knot, ideal with wide spread collars and formal events. Cross the wide end over the front to the left, up through the neck loop and down on the left side. Take it behind the narrow end and around to the right. Bring it up to the center, pass it through the neck loop and drop it on the right. Cross it to the left across the front, up through the neck loop, and down through the front loop. Pull to tighten. Because it needs a lot of fabric, choose a thinner tie, or the knot can look bulky and sit too low.
steps.tip: Best with a spread collar and thin tie
steps.mistake: Using a thick tie for a full Windsor
steps.imagePrompt: A large symmetrical Windsor knot on a dark silk tie with a white dress shirt and spread collar, studio light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: The Pratt knot
steps.narration: Step five. The Pratt, also called the Shelby, has a clean, medium-sized shape. This one begins with the tie turned inside out, so the back of the tie faces you, with the wide end on your right. Pass the wide end under the narrow end to the left, then up through the center toward the neck loop, through the loop, and down to the left. Carry it across the front to the right, push it up into the neck loop from underneath, and down through the front loop. Tighten. It's a favourite for many people because it looks smart without being bulky. Many find it easier to repeat than the Windsor.
steps.tip: Start with the tie inside out
steps.mistake: Forgetting to turn the tie inside out
steps.imagePrompt: A medium symmetrical tie knot on a grey patterned tie, white shirt, close-up, soft daylight, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Tighten and add a dimple
steps.narration: Step six. Once the last pass is done, don't just yank the tie. Hold the knot with one hand and pull the wide end down slowly with the other, to tighten the knot. Then slide the knot up until it sits snugly under your collar. For a neat dimple, pinch the tie just below the knot as you tighten it, so a small fold forms in the center. Adjust the sides until the knot looks even, and fold your collar down around it. Take a second to check it in the mirror from the front, because small adjustments make a big difference to how professional it looks.
steps.tip: Pinch below the knot for a dimple
steps.mistake: Leaving the knot loose and low
steps.imagePrompt: Fingers pinching a tie just below the knot to form a small dimple, white shirt, close-up, soft light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Check length and untie it properly
steps.narration: Step seven. The tip of the wide end should reach your belt buckle, and the narrow end should be hidden behind it. If it's too short, retie the knot with a longer wide end, or try a smaller knot. When the day is over, untie the tie by reversing the steps. Loosen the knot, then take the wide end back out through the loop. Don't pull the narrow end through the knot, because that twists and damages the fabric. Hang the tie, or roll it up, so it stays smooth. A tie that is stored flat or rolled loosely keeps its shape for many years, and recovers from creases much faster.
steps.tip: Tip should touch your belt buckle
steps.mistake: Pulling the narrow end through to untie
steps.imagePrompt: Several neatly hung silk neckties on a wooden rack in a wardrobe, soft light, photorealistic, no text

bonus.label: TROUBLESHOOTING
bonus.title: Fixing a crooked knot
bonus.narration: If your knot leans to one side, one pass was loose, so pull each pass snug. If the seam shows at the front, the tie is twisted, so lay it flat and start again. If the wide end ends up too short, start with the narrow end a little higher.
bonus.tip: Snug every pass before the next
bonus.imagePrompt: A man in a white shirt adjusting a navy tie knot in front of a mirror, face not visible, soft window light. Photorealistic photograph for a how-to video. Bright natural light, clean and uncluttered. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: GO FURTHER
bonus.title: Match the knot to the shirt
bonus.narration: A wide spread collar suits a larger knot, like the Windsor. A narrow collar looks better with a small four-in-hand. The knot should fill the space between the collar points. When in doubt, the half Windsor works with almost everything.
bonus.tip: The half Windsor fits almost anything
bonus.imagePrompt: A white dress shirt with a spread collar and a neatly tied navy tie, shown close up on a wooden table. Photorealistic photograph for a how-to video. Bright natural light, clean and uncluttered. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: KEEP YOUR TIES
bonus.title: Care for your ties
bonus.narration: Never leave a tie knotted overnight, because it stretches the fabric. Hang it on a rack, or roll it loosely in a drawer. Steam out wrinkles in a steamy bathroom, and take silk ties to a dry cleaner instead of scrubbing stains.
bonus.imagePrompt: A wooden wardrobe tie rack with several neatly hung ties in different colors, soft indoor light. Photorealistic photograph for a how-to video. Bright natural light, clean and uncluttered. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, getting the length wrong. A tie that ends above your belt or below it looks off, so adjust before you finish. Second, picking the wrong knot for the tie. Thick ties suit small knots, and thin ones suit larger ones. And third, tightening in a hurry. Slow tightening gives you a smooth knot, while a quick pull gives you a twisted one. Practice a few times, and the muscle memory will soon take over. Watch out for twisted fabric inside the knot, which spoils the look.
items: Ending above or below the belt
Using a large knot with a thick tie
Yanking the knot tight in a hurry

recap.narration: Let's recap. Set up your collar, with the wide end on the right and lower. Learn the quick four-in-hand. Move up to the half Windsor. Try the full Windsor for formal events. Learn the Pratt knot, tied inside out. Tighten slowly and add a dimple. And check the length, then untie the knot properly at the end of the day. Four knots, and you're ready for any occasion. The bonus sections cover crooked knots, matching and tie care.
items: Set up your collar and tie
Check length and untie it properly

outro: That's how you tie a tie, with four classic knots. If this saved your interview or your wedding, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments which knot is your favorite, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow.

metadata.title: How to Tie a Tie: 4 Knots, Step by Step
metadata.description:
Never learned how to tie a tie? In this step-by-step video you'll learn four classic necktie knots: the quick four-in-hand, the balanced half Windsor, the formal full Windsor and the Pratt (Shelby) knot. We start with the right setup and length, show each move clearly, add a dimple, and explain how to untie a tie without damaging it. Perfect for interviews, weddings, school and work. Includes a clear guide to tie length, knot size and a tip for adding a dimple.

You'll need: a shirt with a collar, a necktie, a mirror, a few minutes of patience.

short.title: The easiest tie knot (3 moves) #shorts
short.description: The easiest tie knot: cross, wrap, feed through. Full guide with 4 knots on the channel. #tie #style #howto
short.hook: Can't tie a tie? This knot takes three moves.

steps.title: Cross and wrap
steps.narration: One. Cross the wide end over the narrow end, then behind it and out to the right.

steps.title: Cross again
steps.narration: Two. Carry the wide end across the front to the left.

steps.title: Feed and tighten
steps.narration: Three. Push it up through the neck loop, down through the front loop, and tighten.
